transcript.text: Thank you all for meeting with me today. As you know, an eighth-grade civics class has proposed an oral-history project where students would interview community members about local history. Before I can sign off on this, I'd like to walk through the draft plan together as part of our routine approval process. The plan as I understand it calls for 20 student interviewers, audio recording on personal phones, publication of all recordings on the public school website, and indefinite retention of the files. I'd like to hear from each of you — the project advisor, counselor, and instructional technology coordinator — about any concerns or considerations we should address before I approve this project. Let's start with the project advisor: can you tell me more about the educational goals and how the interviews will be structured?

transcript.text: Thank you, Dr. Morgan. I'm happy to walk through the educational goals. The project aims to engage students in collecting first-hand accounts from longtime community members about how our town has changed over the decades — things like the founding of neighborhood associations, shifts in local businesses, and major civic events. Structurally, each student interviewer would be paired with a community member, conduct a 30-to-45-minute recorded interview using a prepared question guide we develop in class, and then each student would write a short reflection connecting what they heard to a civics concept we've studied. However, I do need to raise an important point regarding the student interviewers before we go further. My project roster review shows that not all 20 students are currently eligible to conduct recorded interviews — there's a training-verification requirement I need to flag for this approval file.
